lesson.text: Quick memory: how many beats does a crotchet last? (One.) Today: your voice, the instrument you always carry.
Stand or sit tall with relaxed shoulders. Good posture gives your lungs room to fill with air.
Breathe low and slow: your tummy moves out as you breathe in. Then let the air out steadily as you sing.
Warm up first, like an athlete: hum, buzz your lips, yawn, and slide your voice from low to high like a siren.
Singing in tune means your notes match the notes you hear. Listen first, then copy. This tune goes up: sing it back.
In an echo song, someone sings a line and you sing it straight back, exactly the same. Listen, then echo.
Look after your voice: drink water, don't shout or strain, and rest it if it feels tired or scratchy.
Try it in the world: stand on a hill in your world and sing a warm-up siren, low to high. Then sing a short tune to a friend and let them echo it back.

exercises.prompt: Why should you stand tall when you sing?
exercises.hint: What do you need lots of to sing?
choices: your lungs have room to fill with air
exercises.explain: Standing tall gives your lungs room to fill with air.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good warm-up for your voice?
exercises.hint: Warm-ups are gentle.
choices: humming and sliding like a siren
shouting as loud as you can
exercises.explain: Humming and sliding your voice like a siren gently gets it ready.

exercises.prompt: Drinking water helps look after your voice.
exercises.hint: Is a dry throat good for singing?
exercises.explain: True: water keeps your voice comfortable.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Does this tune go up or down?
exercises.hint: Draw the tune in the air with your finger as you listen: up for higher notes, down for lower ones.
exercises.explain: It goes up, one step at a time.

exercises.prompt: Listen to the tune and its echo. Did the echo copy it exactly?
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: True: the echo sang the same three notes.

exercises.prompt: Listen to this tune and its echo. Did the echo copy it exactly?
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: False: the echo's middle note was higher than the tune's. In tune means matching every note.

exercises.prompt: How should your tummy move when you breathe in to sing?
exercises.hint: Breathe low, like filling a balloon.
choices: it goes up to your chin
exercises.explain: It moves out, as the air fills your lungs from the bottom.

exercises.prompt: Your voice feels scratchy after singing a lot. What should you do?
exercises.hint: What helps anything that is tired?
exercises.explain: Rest it and drink water. Never strain a tired voice.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for singing well in order.
exercises.hint: Get your body ready first, then your voice, then sing.
exercises.explain: Stand tall, breathe low and slow, warm up with humming, then sing.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Did the echo match the tune?
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: True: the echo sang every note the same.

exercises.prompt: Listen carefully. Did the echo match the tune this time?
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: False: the echo's last note stayed too high. It should have gone down one more step.

exercises.prompt: Listen: someone tries to sing the same note three times. Which one is not in tune?
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: The third note is higher than the other two, so it is not in tune.

exercises.prompt: What does singing in tune mean?
exercises.hint: Think of the echo songs.
choices: your notes match the notes you should sing
exercises.explain: Singing in tune means your notes match the right notes.

exercises.prompt: Why do singers warm up before they sing?
exercises.hint: Athletes warm up too.
choices: to get their voices ready and avoid strain
to use up all their breath
exercises.explain: Warming up gets the voice ready and helps stop it from being strained.

exercises.prompt: Listen. To sing this, your voice has to…
exercises.hint: Hum the notes as you listen. Does your voice go up, go down or stay where it is?
exercises.explain: It leaps up a long way: from a low note to the same note higher up.

exercises.prompt: Good for your voice, or not?
exercises.hint: Would it help your voice or hurt it?
exercises.explain: Water and rest look after your voice; shouting and straining hurt it.

exercises.prompt: Match each warm-up to what you do.
exercises.hint: A siren goes up and down, like a fire engine.
exercises.explain: A hum is sung with closed lips, a siren slides from low to high, and an echo sings a line back.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: good posture for singing, or not?
exercises.hint: Does it give your lungs room to fill?
exercises.explain: Standing tall with relaxed shoulders gives your lungs room; slumping and hunching squash them.

exercises.prompt: Sort the tips: posture, breathing, or looking after your voice?
exercises.hint: Is it about how you stand, how you breathe, or how you keep your voice healthy?
exercises.explain: Posture: stand tall with relaxed shoulders. Breathing: your tummy moves out as you breathe in, and the air goes out steadily. Voice care: drink water and rest a tired voice.

exercises.prompt: Echo this clapped rhythm, as you would echo a sung line.
exercises.hint: Listen to the whole pattern first, then copy it exactly, gaps and all.
exercises.explain: Claps in boxes 1, 3, 5 and 6, rests in the others: an echo copies every sound and every gap exactly, just as in an echo song.
